title: Sell Mineral Rights in Harrison County, WV
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Harrison County, WV | Clarksburg
metaDescription: Own mineral rights in Harrison County, WV, birthplace of the state's gas industry? We buy interests here directly, verified at the Clarksburg courthouse.
heroLead: Harrison County has a claim most counties in the state can't make: Hope Natural Gas Company, one of the earliest and most influential natural gas operators in the country, was founded in Clarksburg in 1898, and the county's mineral ownership record reflects a leasing history that runs longer and deeper than almost anywhere else in West Virginia.
intro: That depth of history is exactly what makes Harrison County mineral ownership complicated. A tract here can carry a lease that predates the First World War, a second lease from the mid-twentieth century, and a third from the modern Marcellus and Utica/Point Pleasant boom, each layered on the same acreage with its own terms and its own operator.

We buy oil and gas mineral and royalty interests throughout Harrison County directly, working from the actual recorded chain of title for your specific tract, whether it sits in Clarksburg proper, a growth corridor like Bridgeport, or a rural community like Gypsy, Despard, or Enterprise, rather than a general county-wide estimate.

sections.heading: Where the modern gas industry effectively began
paragraphs: Hope Natural Gas's founding in Clarksburg set off more than a century of leasing activity across Harrison County. The earliest of those leases, many written as flat-rate agreements paying a fixed annual sum per well, are still technically in force on tracts throughout the county today, having never been formally terminated even as production declined or shifted to newer wells nearby.

For a mineral owner, this history means the recorded lease on your tract may be genuinely old, older than most people assume a 'still active' lease could be, and reading its actual terms matters more here than almost anywhere else in the state.

sections.heading: Growth corridors reshaping the mineral map
paragraphs: Bridgeport's rapid growth around the airport and interstate interchange, and Clarksburg's own suburban expansion into communities like East View and Despard, have subdivided farmland that was leased for gas decades before any development plat existed. In many of these areas, the mineral rights were reserved separately from the surface at the time of sale, leaving a mineral estate that no longer matches any current residential or commercial lot line.
Confirming ownership on these tracts means tracing the original farm parcel description through to the modern development, a step we take before ever naming a number.

sections.heading: Flat-rate leases and the conversion statute
paragraphs: West Virginia requires flat-rate gas leases to convert to a statutory minimum of one-eighth royalty on production, but that conversion only applies when it's actually flagged and processed. Given how many of Harrison County's leases originate from the earliest era of the state's gas industry, we treat every older lease as a candidate for conversion review rather than assuming the family's current flat payment is all they're entitled to.

sections.heading: Modern Marcellus and Utica development
paragraphs: Harrison County has remained an active target for operators pursuing both Marcellus and deeper Utica/Point Pleasant zones, particularly in the towns and rural communities surrounding Clarksburg. A single tract can carry a legacy lease and a modern pooled unit interest simultaneously, and we read both instruments separately since they rarely share the same royalty structure.

sections.heading: Heirship across a century of ownership
paragraphs: With leasing activity this old, mineral tracts have typically split across four, five, or more generations of a single family, producing interests with a dozen or more record owners spread across multiple states, several unreachable, some deceased without a probated estate. We buy individual heir shares without requiring the whole family to sell together, and we handle the chain-of-title work, tracing wills, intestate succession, and prior deeds, as part of the purchase.

faqs.question: How old can an active Harrison County lease actually be?
faqs.answer: Some tracts carry leases dating to the founding of Hope Natural Gas in the late 1890s, still technically in force. We can trace and evaluate instruments this old.

faqs.question: My family's tract near Bridgeport was subdivided for development. Do we still own the minerals?
faqs.answer: If the mineral rights were properly reserved when the land was sold, yes. We verify the reservation deed and current record owner before making an offer.

faqs.question: Is my old flat-rate lease eligible for the statutory conversion to a royalty?
faqs.answer: It depends on the specific lease language and whether conversion has already been applied. We check every Harrison County lease individually.

faqs.question: Can a tract have both a legacy lease and a modern Marcellus unit interest?
faqs.answer: Yes, that's common given the county's long leasing history. We review both instruments separately since terms usually differ.

faqs.question: How many heirs are typical on a century-old Harrison County interest?
faqs.answer: It varies, but interests with this much history commonly involve eight to fifteen or more co-owners across several states.

faqs.question: What paperwork speeds up an offer on a Harrison County interest?
faqs.answer: A copy of any deed, lease, or probate document you have is useful, but we can usually locate the recorded chain of title ourselves through the Clarksburg courthouse once we have your name and the general tract location.

faqs.question: Do you handle interests spread across several communities within the county?
faqs.answer: Yes, whether your family's interest sits in Clarksburg itself or in a smaller community like Bridgeport, Gypsy, or Hepzibah, we evaluate each tract on its own recorded history.
